learningObjectives.title: Jewish social action and care for others

questions.q: What does the Hebrew word 'tzedakah' literally mean?
questions.explain: Tzedakah comes from the root 'tzedek', meaning justice or righteousness, showing that charity is seen as a duty of justice rather than mere generosity.

questions.q: Which Jewish scholar set out the famous eight levels (or 'ladder') of tzedakah?
questions.explain: The medieval scholar Maimonides described eight ascending degrees of charitable giving in his writings.

questions.q: According to Maimonides, what is the highest level of tzedakah?
options: Helping someone become self-sufficient so they no longer need charity
Giving a very large public donation
Giving cheerfully but only a small amount
questions.explain: The greatest form of giving strengthens a person through a gift, loan, partnership or job so they can support themselves.

questions.q: Which of these is considered the lowest level of tzedakah by Maimonides?
questions.explain: Giving reluctantly or with a bad grace is regarded as the least worthy form of charity, though still better than not giving at all.

questions.q: In Maimonides' ladder, why is giving where neither the giver nor the recipient knows the other's identity valued so highly?
options: It protects the dignity of the person receiving help
It allows the donor to be publicly praised
It means less money needs to be given
It removes any duty to give again
questions.explain: Anonymous, double-blind giving avoids embarrassing the recipient and prevents the donor seeking status, preserving human dignity.

questions.q: The command 'Justice, justice shall you pursue' (tzedek, tzedek tirdof) comes from which part of the Torah?
questions.explain: Deuteronomy 16:20 commands Jews actively to pursue justice, underpinning the link between charity and social justice.

questions.q: In Jewish law, what is 'pe'ah'?
options: Leaving the corners of a field unharvested for the poor
A tithe paid to the priests
A prayer said before giving charity
questions.explain: The Torah commands farmers to leave the corners (pe'ah) of their fields so the poor and the stranger can gather food.

questions.q: The practice of 'leket' involves leaving what for the poor to collect?
options: Gleanings, the crops dropped during harvesting
Money placed in a collection box
questions.explain: Leket refers to fallen ears of grain left where they drop so that the poor may glean them freely.

questions.q: What is a 'pushke' (tzedakah box) used for?
questions.explain: A pushke or tzedakah box is a container kept in many Jewish homes for regularly setting aside money to give to those in need.

questions.q: As a traditional guideline, what proportion of their income do many observant Jews aim to give to charity?
questions.explain: The custom of ma'aser, giving a tenth of one's income, reflects the biblical idea of tithing for those in need.

questions.q: What does 'gemilut hasadim' mean?
questions.explain: Gemilut hasadim describes practical acts of loving kindness, such as visiting the sick or comforting mourners, which go beyond giving money.

questions.q: The command 'Love your neighbour as yourself' is found in which book of the Torah?
questions.explain: Leviticus 19:18 contains this teaching, often cited as a foundation for Jewish care and concern for others.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'tikkun olam' mean?
questions.explain: Tikkun olam literally means 'repair of the world' and expresses the duty to improve society and creation.

questions.q: The idea of tikkun olam expresses the belief that human beings are…
options: Partners with God in repairing and improving the world
Unable to change the world at all
Responsible only for their own families
questions.explain: Tikkun olam teaches that people share responsibility with God for healing the world's brokenness through good actions.

questions.q: How does belief in tikkun olam encourage Jewish social action?
options: It teaches that Jews have a duty to help improve society and the world
It teaches that the world cannot be changed
It teaches that only prayer matters
It teaches that wealth should be hoarded
questions.explain: Because the world is seen as unfinished and repairable, tikkun olam motivates Jews to work actively for justice and the good of others.

questions.q: A Jewish business owner gives an unemployed man a job so he can support his family without depending on charity. Which level of tzedakah does this best show?
options: The highest level, helping someone become self-sufficient
questions.explain: Providing employment enables self-reliance, which Maimonides ranks as the greatest form of charitable help.

questions.q: A Jewish farmer deliberately leaves the edges of his field unharvested so poor families can gather food. Which Torah practice is he following?
questions.explain: Leaving the corners of the field for the poor and the stranger is the biblical practice of pe'ah.

questions.q: A group of Jewish teenagers regularly volunteer at a food bank to help vulnerable people in their town. Which idea best explains their motivation?
options: Tikkun olam, working to repair and improve the world
Brit milah, the covenant of circumcision
questions.explain: Practical work to relieve need reflects the duty of tikkun olam to help mend the world through social action.

questions.q: A woman donates to a charity in a way that means neither she nor the family she helps ever learns the other's identity. What does this show about her giving?
options: It reflects one of the highest forms of tzedakah because it protects dignity
It is the lowest form because the gift is hidden
It does not count as tzedakah
questions.explain: Anonymous giving where neither party knows the other is highly praised by Maimonides for preserving the recipient's dignity.

questions.q: The Torah repeatedly commands Jews to show particular care for which vulnerable groups?
options: The widow, the orphan and the stranger
questions.explain: Scripture singles out the widow, orphan and stranger as those most in need of protection and support, shaping Jewish social action.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Religious Studies (0490) syllabus; Judaism: Religion & Social Action
